newsitem.title: GERMANY: German builders protest against unemployment.
newsitem.headline: German builders protest against unemployment.

text.p: Thousands of German construction workers protested for the fourth consecutive day in Berlin on Thursday against chronic unemployment in their sector and so-called "wage-dumping" by foreign firms.
Negotiators meeting in Frankfurt said they saw little chance of a deal in the latest round of wage talks for the sector. They agreed to meet again on March 25 to make a fresh attempt.
A 25 billion mark ($14.57 billion) investment drive unveiled by Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Wednesday did little to placate the workers.

Earlier on Thursday, Kohl and mining union leader Hans Berger reached a compromise to avoid mass layoffs while sharply cutting back subsidies to the coal industry. Miners who had besieged Bonn for three days began to return home.
Police said about 4,000 construction workers marched from the Potsdamer Platz, Europe's biggest building site, to the area where the new German Finance Ministry is being built.
Thousands of workers have been holding a vigil for four days on the Potsdamer Platz, due to become a glitzy shopping, business and apartment complex in the new German capital.
Opposition Social Democrat (SPD) party manager Franz Muentefering called on the construction workers to continue their demonstrations against government policies.
"Show that your interests are those of all the unemployed people in this country," he told them.

Unions expect this week's protests to reach a climax on Friday when workers will be addressed by a leading SDP member, Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder, and German Trade Union Federation (DGB) head Dieter Schulte.
Miners from the coal-producing Ruhr region and players from first division soccer team Schalke also joined the protests.

The IG Bau building workers' union is seeking new clauses compensating workers for pay lost as a result of poor weather and the reinstatement of a "13th month" bonus that employers have cancelled from existing contracts.
The union also wants to stop foreigners illegally working on construction sites and undercutting wages.
IG Bau has not yet specified its wage demands but says its aim is that wages should not fall in real terms.
The union estimates there are 1.3 million currently employed in the building sector and a further 400,000 are out of work.

Economists said Kohl's investment package, set to be approved next week, would not change their growth forecasts for 1997 and would make no real dent in Germany's record post-war unemployment level of 4.7 million.

Analysts said public construction investment accounted for only a small proportion -- around 15 percent in 1995 -- of overall construction spending and that the package was largely a political measure. ($1=1.7153 Mark)
